# Sample Size for ROC Curve and AUC {#sec-auc-planning}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- State the diagnostic objective for an AUC.
- Explain how diseased and non-diseased counts affect AUC precision.
:::

## The idea

The area under an ROC curve (AUC) summarises rank discrimination across thresholds. Planning to **estimate** AUC requires a precision target, while testing against a reference AUC requires a null value, anticipated value, alpha and power. Traditional Hanley–McNeil approximations express the AUC variance as a function of AUC and counts of reference-standard-positive and reference-standard-negative participants.

## When and how to apply it

An AUC calculation does not replace planning based on sensitivity at a clinically chosen threshold, calibration, positive predictive value or decision utility. Disease spectrum, reference-standard quality and intended use influence interpretation.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A clinical biomarker is expected to achieve AUC 0.80. Specify whether the aim is a confidence interval of half-width 0.05 or a test of AUC against 0.65.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Using an AUC of 0.80 without planning the diseased and non-diseased composition can produce a misleading total sample size.
:::
